description: Schematic engineering-stress versus strain graph, not numerical experimental data. Stress uses initial area. Preserve O-A-B-C-D-E-K, Q/P and all solid guides; B is below the C-D plateau. The post-maximum drop includes necking and decreasing load capacity, not material softening alone. No true-stress curve.

authoritativeText.text:
51. 强度　安全系数

建造房屋、桥梁、飞机、汽车和轮船时，需要了解混凝土、钢、塑料等材料的强度。
仅知道小形变时的刚度还不够，还要了解较大形变、卸载以及最终破坏时的行为。
这些性质主要通过针对具体材料、样品和加载条件的实验获得。

**比例极限和弹性极限**
材料可以通过拉伸或压缩实验检验；
本节随后讨论一类延性样品的单轴拉伸示意，拉伸与压缩的曲线不必相同。

测量样品的伸长量和所受拉力，绘制应力 $\sigma$ 与相对伸长量 $\varepsilon$ 的关系，得到拉伸图，如图88。
这里的纵轴采用拉力除以初始横截面积的工程应力，横轴采用长度增量除以初始标距的工程应变；
不能把纵轴当作按颈缩后的实际面积计算的真应力。

在线弹性比例区，应力 $\sigma$ 与 $\varepsilon$ 成正比，对应图中 $OA$ 段。
在所采用的实验条件和比例判据下，仍满足这种胡克定律比例关系的最大应力，叫做比例极限。



图 88

超过比例极限后，应力与相对伸长量不再成正比；
但非线性并不必然意味着已经产生明显的永久形变。
图中的 $AB$ 段示意这种区别：卸去负载后，样品仍可近似恢复原来的尺寸。

原书以卸载后的相对剩余形变不超过0.1%作为“不产生明显剩余形变”的判据，并把按此判据确定的最大应力称为弹性极限。
这个剩余形变阈值是本书采用的约定，不能当作所有材料和实验共同遵循的精确标准。
原书又说弹性极限只超过比例极限的百分之一，这是其说明中的近似量；

两者的差值并不是所有样品都相同的固定比例。

**强度极限和安全系数**
对本节图示的这类材料，超过弹性极限后卸去负载，样品虽然会缩短一部分，却可能留下不能恢复的伸长。
卸载后保留下来的永久形变称为塑性形变，应与可以恢复的弹性部分区分。

这并不要求所有材料在达到某一应力后，都出现相同的塑性阶段。

继续加载时，塑性伸长可能明显增加。
图中 $C$ 点附近开始的屈服平台示意：在相应加载条件下，拉力近似不增加，样品仍能发生较明显的伸长。
原书把这称为材料的“流动性”，对应近似水平的 $CD$ 段；

这里是固体的塑性屈服，不是材料变成了液体。
明显的平台只出现在某些材料及实验条件下，不能要求所有拉伸曲线都有这样的水平段。

随后，随形变 $\varepsilon$ 增大，图示样品的应变硬化使工程应力曲线上升，到 $E$ 点达到最大值。
此后可能发生颈缩，工程应力曲线下降，直到样品在点 $K$ 断裂。
在这种拉伸实验中，最大工程应力 $\sigma_{\text{极限}}$ 叫做本节的强度极限；

图示样品的断裂发生在最大值之后。
颈缩时，试样局部截面不断减小，继续伸长所需的拉力可以下降；
纵轴仍用初始面积计算，因此曲线下降并不表示颈缩处的真应力也必定下降。

原书“不增加外界负载，样品被拉得很长”的描述不能理解为断裂阶段的拉力必须严格不变。
强度极限和曲线形状随材料、加工状态及测试条件变化，脆性材料不一定经历同样的屈服、硬化和颈缩过程。

为了留出强度裕量，本节把结构的许用应力 $\sigma_{\text{许用}}$ 取在材料强度极限以下。
原书按强度极限与许用应力的比值定义安全系数：
$n=\frac{\sigma_{\text{极限}}}{\sigma_{\text{许用}}}$。

（6-6）
在这种校核中，实际工作应力应不超过许用应力。
不过，低于强度极限或具有这个比值，并不能单独证明整座建筑或结构安全，还需考虑变形、稳定、疲劳和连接等其他可能的失效条件。

安全系数的选择与材料性质、静载或动载、破坏后果以及条件的不确定性等因素有关。
原书给出 $1.7\sim10$ 的区间，作为其工程说明中的范围；
这不是适用于所有结构的固定取值范围，也不是本课提供的通用设计标准。

在具体工程中按相应条件确定安全系数后，可依照本节的定义，用公式（6-6）确定对应的许用应力。
这里保留的是定义及其作用，不能仅凭原书的示例区间完成实际结构的安全判定。

51. Strength and Factor of Safety

Building houses, bridges, aircraft, cars, and ships requires knowledge of the strength of concrete, steel, plastics, and other materials.
Knowing stiffness at small deformations is not enough: behavior at larger deformation, during unloading, and at eventual failure also matters.
These properties are mainly obtained through experiments on particular materials, specimens, and loading conditions.

**Proportional limit and elastic limit**
Materials can be tested in tension or compression.
The following diagram represents uniaxial tension of one kind of ductile specimen;

tensile and compressive curves need not be identical.
Measuring specimen extension and tensile force gives a graph of stress $\sigma$ against relative extension $\varepsilon$, as in Figure 88.

Here the ordinate is engineering stress, the tensile force divided by the original cross-sectional area;
the abscissa is engineering strain, the increase in length divided by the original gauge length.

The ordinate must not be confused with true stress calculated using the actual area after necking.
In the linear elastic proportional region, stress $\sigma$ is proportional to $\varepsilon$, represented by segment $OA$.
For the experimental conditions and proportionality criterion used, the greatest stress still satisfying this proportional form of Hooke's law is called the proportional limit.



Figure 88

Beyond the proportional limit, stress and relative extension are no longer proportional.
Nonlinearity, however, does not necessarily mean that appreciable permanent deformation has occurred.

Segment $AB$ illustrates this distinction: after unloading, the specimen can still approximately recover its original dimensions.
The textbook takes a residual relative deformation after unloading of no more than 0.1% as its criterion for no appreciable residual deformation, and calls the greatest stress satisfying this criterion the elastic limit.

This threshold is the convention used in this book, not an exact standard shared by every material and experiment.
The textbook also states that the elastic limit exceeds the proportional limit by only one percent;
this is an approximate value in its explanation, not a fixed percentage difference for every specimen.

**Ultimate strength and factor of safety**
For the kind of material shown here, unloading beyond the elastic limit may shorten the specimen somewhat but leave extension that cannot be recovered.

The permanent deformation remaining after unloading is called plastic deformation and must be distinguished from the recoverable elastic part.
This does not require every material to enter the same plastic stages after reaching some particular stress.

Continued loading may produce appreciably greater plastic extension.
The yield plateau beginning near point $C$ represents conditions in which the tensile force remains approximately unchanged while the specimen can continue to extend noticeably.

The textbook calls this behavior "flow," represented by the nearly horizontal segment $CD$.
This is plastic yielding of a solid, not conversion of the material into a liquid.

A pronounced plateau occurs only for certain materials and experimental conditions;
not every tensile curve must contain such a horizontal segment.

As deformation $\varepsilon$ then increases, strain hardening of the illustrated specimen raises the engineering-stress curve to its maximum at point $E$.
Necking may follow, and the engineering-stress curve falls until the specimen fractures at point $K$.

In this tensile experiment, the maximum engineering stress $\sigma_{\text{ultimate}}$ is the ultimate strength discussed here.
Fracture of the illustrated specimen occurs after the maximum.

During necking, the local cross section decreases, and the tensile force needed for further extension can fall.
Because the ordinate still uses the original area, a falling curve does not mean that the true stress at the neck necessarily falls as well.

The textbook description of large extension without an increase in external load must not be understood as requiring strictly constant tensile force throughout fracture.
Ultimate strength and curve shape depend on material, processing, and test conditions;
brittle materials need not undergo the same sequence of yielding, hardening, and necking.

To provide a strength margin, this lesson takes the allowable stress $\sigma_{\text{allowable}}$ of a structure below the ultimate strength of its material.
The textbook defines the factor of safety as the ratio of ultimate strength to allowable stress:
$n=\frac{\sigma_{\text{ultimate}}}{\sigma_{\text{allowable}}}$.

(6-6)
In this check, the actual working stress should not exceed the allowable stress.

However, staying below ultimate strength or having this ratio does not by itself prove that an entire building or structure is safe;
deformation, stability, fatigue, connections, and other possible failure conditions also matter.

The choice of a factor of safety depends on material properties, static or dynamic loading, consequences of failure, uncertainty, and other conditions.
The textbook gives the interval $1.7\sim10$ as a range within its engineering explanation.

This is not a fixed range for every structure or a universal design standard supplied by this lesson.
Once a factor of safety has been chosen for the relevant engineering conditions, formula (6-6) determines the corresponding allowable stress according to this definition.

The definition and its role are retained here;
the illustrative range alone is insufficient for assessing the safety of a real structure.
